sources.title: AI Tinkerers One-Shot: How to Ship Complex Features 10x Faster with AI Agents
sources.note: Local faster-whisper machine transcript, no speaker labels; host Joe Heitzeberg; carded Dex only by content. Not listed under this title in the inventory (only the Build Wiz recap of it is).

sources.title: Mastra Agents Hour: The Software Factory, Dex Horthy on Shipping Fast Without AI Slop
sources.note: Local machine transcript, no speaker labels; Mastra hosts' questions not carded. Inventory July 2026 lists the Mastra page.

sources.title: Build Wiz AI Show: How to Ship Complex Features 10x Faster with AI Agents
sources.note: AI two-voice recap of the AI Tinkerers episode; read the opening only, used just to cross-check mishearings (apparatus/harness, use effect). Not carded.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: don't use prompts for control flow. If you know the workflow, make the parts that are deterministic
cards.claim: Where the workflow is known, make steps deterministic code with small LLM steps inside rather than steering the sequence with prompt text.
cards.evidence_detail: Based on founders he interviewed building enterprise AI (legal, fintech, insurance, compliance tech).
cards.landing: Phase routine enforced by scripts or hooks, not prose

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: That prompt has 50 to 100 instructions in it, and the design and the structure would get skipped all the time.
cards.claim: A single create-plan prompt carrying design, structure and plan instructions got steps skipped, so he split it into separate prompts and context windows (a change from the one-prompt RPI planning step).
cards.evidence_detail: Observed while rolling RPI out to many users; no counts.
cards.landing: Split the phase routine into separate fresh-context steps; shorter always-loaded rules

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: repeat the instructions at the beginning, and then you repeat the important ones at the end.
cards.claim: The old workaround for long planning prompts was to repeat important instructions at start and end, which he now calls a bad product experience and replaced with a split workflow.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md trim; do not rely on repetition

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we're forcing the human into the parts of the workflow where thinking is required.
cards.claim: The workflow places human review only at thinking-heavy steps (design discussion, structure outline) and automates the rest.
cards.landing: Owner checkpoints at design and plan, not every step

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you can't outsource the thinking. AI cannot replace thinking. It can only amplify your thinking
cards.claim: AI amplifies thinking or its absence; skipping the human thinking step yields poorly thought-out code (he saw it in a demo run the night before).

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we do not include the ticket in that context, fresh context window, just the questions.
cards.claim: Ticket becomes research questions; research runs in a fresh context given only the questions, so the research stays objective and carries no implementation intent (refinement of RPI).
cards.evidence_detail: Found after intent leaked into research docs; no numbers.
cards.landing: Research step of phase routine and the P1 cold-resume test

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if you tell it how to write code and you tell it to go research, it's going to get steered
cards.claim: Coding rules loaded during research steer the model toward making changes, so research documents leak opinions; coding rules should not be in context during research.
cards.evidence_detail: Experience; he is unsure whether such rules belong in CLAUDE.md or elsewhere.
cards.landing: Move coding rules out of always-loaded CLAUDE.md; load per phase

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you don't really know bad patterns until they burn you and then you go put in your golden rules
cards.claim: Golden rules come from patterns that burned you; where they live (CLAUDE.md or elsewhere) and when they are pulled into context is still unsettled.
cards.evidence_detail: Cites a Netflix engineer's talk; Dex admits open question.
cards.landing: Invariants section of CLAUDE.md and its trim

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Dynamically generating that context by doing research to your code base is a more effective way
cards.claim: Research run per ticket by sub-agents replaces a hand-maintained, always-loaded context file because the file always drifts; research can also target an open source repo or the web.
cards.evidence_detail: Argued; the 'more effective' phrasing is the host's, Dex shows the research animation.
cards.landing: Knowledge-store pilot; trim CLAUDE.md in favour of on-demand research

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: launch a bunch of sub-agents to do these, like, vertical slices through the code base.
cards.claim: Research dispatches sub-agents on vertical slices of the codebase and writes one compacted research document.
cards.evidence_detail: Shown in a demo; no numbers.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the agentic rag thing which is basically Claude models plus grep is pretty good sometimes a little slower
cards.claim: He prefers slow and reliable agentic search (grep plus model) over optimised retrieval for codebase understanding.
cards.landing: Keep the Haiku file locator plain; no call-graph tooling

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: at every one of these stages we're compacting context
cards.claim: Each stage compacts context into a document with a specific output format, and later stages deterministically allocate the existing docs into the next context window.
cards.landing: Phase hand-off documents (Plan @ sha journal) as designed compaction

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: So we're getting right now is level three which is like you are at each step check the results
cards.claim: He describes four levels of autonomy: per-step human advance, a fourth that double-runs research and design for variants, a mid level that automates after the structure outline, and full auto.
cards.landing: Per-task autonomy setting in the phase routine

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: If you don't like that, then it rewinds you to the design discussion.
cards.claim: Try the one-shot version first; if the result is poor, rewind to the design discussion and lower the autonomy level rather than start over.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: models really like to make what I like call horizontal plans
cards.claim: Models default to horizontal plans (DB, then service, then API, then UI) with nothing checkable until the end; require vertical tracer-bullet phases validated at each step.
cards.evidence_detail: Observed pattern; credits Pragmatic Programmers and Matt Pocock.
cards.landing: Plan template: vertical phases, each verifiable

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: wire it all the way end to end with no logic, very simple logic
cards.claim: Tracer bullets: wire the feature end to end with mock logic first, then add logic in further vertical passes.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the structure outline is going to have the testing strategy built into it.
cards.claim: The structure outline carries the testing strategy and is ordered so each step can be checked, a shorter alignment document than the long RPI plan.
cards.landing: Plan @ sha body: test strategy per phase

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: The plans really ended up being really long for people to read.
cards.claim: Full RPI plans (a thousand lines) were too long for human alignment, so a short outline with current state, desired state, patterns, design summary and phases is reviewed instead.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: patterns to follow gets surface at the top.
cards.claim: The design discussion template surfaces patterns to follow from the codebase so the human can reject an old pattern (for example six ways to do atomic inserts) before planning.
cards.evidence_detail: Demo; replaces reading the whole objective research doc.
cards.landing: Plan template section: patterns to follow

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I rarely read these anymore
cards.claim: He rarely reads the research document himself, which makes it a model-to-model hand-off, while still reading the design discussion and answering its questions.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I prefer this. ... a flat file with option A, option B
cards.claim: He answers design questions in a flat file (often by voice) instead of the ask-user-question tool, because it is faster and allows pointing at other code.
cards.landing: Owner answers in PR body or file

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Specs have way more impact than the plan has way more impact than the actual coding cycles.
cards.claim: Leverage is ordered spec, then plan, then coding; he says planning gives about 3x and research about 3x, roughly 9 to 10x together.
cards.landing: Spend owner time on spec and plan

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you should learn to be happy with 10 times leverage
cards.claim: Do not automate everything; take the 3x gains, fix the last mile only when it becomes the bottleneck, to avoid meta-tooling soup.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the Ralph Wiggum is like the specs have to be good ... problem has to be verifiable
cards.claim: Autonomous loops only pay off with good specs and a verifiable problem; otherwise they run diligently and produce something not useful (compiler example).
cards.evidence_detail: Cites Geoffrey Huntley's language project; no numbers beyond his remarks.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: If the agent can write the code, the agent can review the code.
cards.claim: A pre-PR agent review step is just another workflow step, so AI review bots add little beyond a well-honed prompt.
cards.landing: Pre-PR reviewer step in the workflow

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: every couple months ... you will hit a moment where you will have a bug that the model cannot solve
cards.claim: Skimping on code attention gives about three months of 3x speed, then a bug the model cannot solve and a week of cleanup; patterns the model sees leak in (React useEffect).
cards.evidence_detail: Team experience of ignoring code for 1-2 months, then rewriting parts.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Models can code. Models can't ship.
cards.claim: Shipping (test, deploy, fix, keep maintainable and non-thrashy) is the engineer's job; the role moves from writing to producing.
cards.evidence_detail: Opinion; attributes the coding vs shipping line to another.
cards.landing: Closing-message questions focus on shipped outcomes

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I'll usually just work two of these in parallel
cards.claim: He runs at most two hard-feature workflows in parallel, cannot do five, and stays away from parallelism bragging; small bugs go to a hands-off assistant.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: 20, 30% if you're just like mostly doing it
cards.claim: Larger teams measure about 20 to 30 percent productivity gain from AI coding versus the 10x solo claim; his target is 2 to 3x on hard code.
cards.evidence_detail: Figures relayed from conversations with team customers (mid-conversation, unclear which speaker states the 20-30%); target of 2-3x is his.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we put artifacts in a separate repo ... treat it as like an S3 bucket
cards.claim: Research and design artifacts are written to a separate synced repo (write hook auto-syncs) and attached to the ticket, treated as revision-history storage rather than real VCS.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we found a bunch of issues with it. ... refined that workflow even more.
cards.claim: He retires RPI as taught in August 2025 for ticket, questions, research, design discussion, structure outline, plan, worktree implementation, PR (five human-facing steps).
cards.evidence_detail: Change of position stated; issues named are the intent-leak and skipped-steps.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Claude likes to use the use effect hook and react.
cards.claim: Frequent model idioms become hard-to-debug patterns; the longer the model sees them the more they leak in.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: have a really good way to preview stuff and poke around at it and send it to someone else
cards.claim: Build infrastructure for previewing a change (preview deploys, sandbox) and make it dead simple to share, since human testing is the bottleneck.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I don't think it's worth trying to get to perfect
cards.claim: Browser-agent testing is improving but he does not pursue perfect automated validation; taste and customer understanding stay human.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: legacy for AI is like anything older than six months
cards.claim: For AI, codebases older than about six months already behave like legacy, so research on existing patterns matters even for young repos.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: GitHub actions is a really good way to do serverless on a cron
cards.claim: He runs headless Claude Code from GitHub Actions on a cron over a markdown CRM repo for routine automation.

cards.source_title: Mastra Agents Hour: The Software Factory
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the code is cheaper now, but the review isn't cheaper.
cards.claim: Code generation is cheap but review is not, so aim for PRs that are 95 to 99 percent correct on arrival; teams are drowning in bad PRs, not PRs.
cards.evidence_detail: Rule of thumb; says unprompted PRs need about 50% rework, 20% rework 'generous'.

cards.source_title: Mastra Agents Hour: The Software Factory
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if you can re-steer early in the process before the model's already committed to a direction
cards.claim: Re-steering early (design discussion, plan) beats fixing after the build, which cuts a six-hour review to 5 or 20 minutes.

cards.source_title: Mastra Agents Hour: The Software Factory
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: don't sacrifice the architecture planning, don't sacrifice the sprint planning, and don't sacrifice the code review.
cards.claim: A lights-off software factory (no code reading) degrades the codebase after 3 to 6 months; keep architecture planning, goal planning and code review.
cards.evidence_detail: His team built one in Sept 2025 and watched it decay over roughly nine months.
cards.landing: Keep human gates; no unattended merge

cards.source_title: Mastra Agents Hour: The Software Factory
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: nowhere in here in the verification loop are we able to punish the model for bad code design
cards.claim: Coding benchmarks (SWE-bench style) and test-pass rewards give no penalty for maintainability, so models are not trained to avoid sloppy design; the verifier cannot be only tests.
cards.evidence_detail: His thesis from reading about RL training, no experiment.
cards.landing: Verifiers must judge design, not just tests

cards.source_title: Mastra Agents Hour: The Software Factory
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: hand issue 21 to Sonnet or even Haiku and see can a smaller dumber model solve an issue
cards.claim: A long-horizon benchmark (about 20 stacked feature requests, Harbor adapter) hands a later issue to a smaller model to measure the code quality the first model left behind.
cards.evidence_detail: Benchmark being built, no results given.

cards.source_title: Mastra Agents Hour: The Software Factory
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you have the inner harness that the labs build ... and then you have the outer harness that you engineer
cards.claim: Harness engineering is split into the inner harness (agent builder's) and the outer harness (feedback loops you engineer as part of the software factory).
cards.evidence_detail: Definition; he argues to defend useful terms against dilution.

cards.source_title: Mastra Agents Hour: The Software Factory
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Agentic code review ... the bottleneck moved
cards.claim: With agents building, the backlog becomes a review backlog, so add agentic code review and agentic browser testing to raise the floor before the human looks.

cards.source_title: Mastra Agents Hour: The Software Factory
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: even if the agent only one shot's like 30% of those, that's 30% of time
cards.claim: Route support tickets and Sentry errors straight into the tracker for an agent to attempt, accepting about 30 percent one-shot success as a win.

cards.source_title: Mastra Agents Hour: The Software Factory
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: anything you can do with deterministic [checks] is great
cards.claim: Deterministic checks and agentic review are good, but if they are the only plan the codebase devolves; planning must precede them.

cards.source_title: Mastra Agents Hour: The Software Factory
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Specdriven dev ... now means a hundred different things
cards.claim: He warns that agent, spec-driven dev, harness engineering and software factory are being diluted into meaningless terms; define them before adopting.

cards.source_title: Mastra Agents Hour: The Software Factory
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Do not use if you are allergic to reasoning about complex systems.
cards.claim: Human Layer is now marketed as an AI IDE and collaboration platform claiming engineers on hard codebases move two to three times faster across the SDLC through design review before agents run.
cards.evidence_detail: Launch video; hundreds of engineers claimed, no data.

cards.source_title: Mastra Agents Hour: The Software Factory
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: The ceremonies have decreased ... planning still has to happen
cards.claim: A Mastra host says that skipped architecture planning makes slop fester; Dex adds that review comments are really aimed at the author's agent, so a human reviewer need not be gentle.
cards.evidence_detail: Host's team practice; Dex endorses planning point.

gaps: Both machine transcripts have no speaker labels and distil-large-v3 errors; the 20-30% team gain (R54-29) and R54-48 may be a guest/host remark.
Levels of autonomy are partly garbled in the AI Tinkerers transcript ('level three', 'four modes').
No SlopCodeBench or effort-level content in this bundle, so L1 is only indirect.
Mastra sections of the transcript on benchmark RL mechanism (reward shaping) were carded only as the headline thesis.

new_sources.title: Geoffrey Huntley programming language build (cursed lang repo) referenced as example of verifiable specs
new_sources.why: Dex cites its specs as the model of good specs for autonomous loops
